name: San Ildefonso Tultepec Otomi, 'Northern Otomi'
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Palancar, Enrique L. 2013. Preaspiration in Northern Otomi: A relic of an old fortis/lenis contrast. In Jean Léo Léonard & Samia Naïm (eds.), Base articulatoire arrière / Backing and Backness (LINCOM Studies in Phonology 01), 205–220. Munich: LINCOM Europa. Open preprint: HAL hal-00920515 (submitted 18 Dec 2013),https://hal.science/hal-00920515/document
catalog_locator: HAL preprint §1.1 'Introduction to Otomi', preprint p. 4, examples (3)–(5); preprint p. 6 rule (15) 'trochaic word'; preprint p. 7 ex. (19) proclitic + stem; preprint p. 9 'wrong stress'; identity statement preprint p. 2 and tone fn. 2 p. 2. Published pagination 205–220 not verified against the LINCOM volume.
catalog_quote: Finally, most lexical words in Northern Otomi are disyllabic in prosodic structure. For this type of words, there is a default stress rule by which stress falls on the first syllable, as in (3). In these examples, as elsewhere, stress is indicated with underlining. (3) pǒ.nt'i 'blessing' / bɘ.hɔi 'mud' / dé.he 'water' / da.da 'old man' / kí̵.t'a '5' / kó.do 'turkey' / gó.hó '4' / etc. [first syllables underlined] As the rule has a default application across the lexicon, deviating patterns like the one illustrated by the words in (4), should be accounted for as being lexically specified. (4) pá.da 'vulture' / bã.t͡si 'child' / gó.né 'dumb' [second syllables underlined] Most of the words with more than one syllable which are still morphologically simple are loanwords, and as such they commonly receive the stress of Spanish, like in (5), whose stress pattern in coherent with the native one in (3). (5) á.bwé.lí.tá 'granny' [lí underlined] ... [p. 6] (15) Preaspiration rule 1: When /p,t,k/ occur as the onset of the weak syllable of a trochaic word, the strong syllable obligatorily receives an aspiration in its coda in the form of an [h]. ... [p. 7] Similarly, as expected by rule 1 no preaspiration occurs when the target word is preceded by a proclitic of TAM and person of the subject, like in (19). This is because the stress falls in the first syllable of the verbal stem, which for most cases corresponds to the lexical root.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (HAL hal-00920515, 17 pp., text) opened and read. The three quoted sentences are present verbatim: PDF page 5 (= preprint p. 4, section 1.1) "Finally, most lexical words in Northern Otomi are disyllabic in prosodic structure. For this type of words, there is a default stress rule by which stress falls on the first syllable, as in (3). In these examples, as elsewhere, stress is indicated with underlining." and "As the rule has a default application across the lexicon, deviating patterns like the one illustrated by the words in (4), should be accounted for as being lexically specified."; PDF page 8 (= preprint p. 7) "This is because the stress falls in the first syllable of the verbal st…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default stress on the first syllable of the (typically disyllabic) lexical word/stem, i.e. a trochaic word (Palancar calls the initial syllable the 'strong syllable of a trochaic word'). TAM/person proclitics fall outside the stress domain, so in inflected verbs stress sits on the first syllable of the verbal stem, which is normally the lexical root — a root-initial pattern could equally be filed as 'morphologically determined'. The rule is a lexical default, not exceptionless.
new_statements.exceptions: Lexically specified second-syllable stress in a few native words, ex. (4): pá.da 'vulture', bã.tsi 'child', gó.né 'dumb' (second syllable underlined in the PDF, checked on the rendered page); Spanish loanwords commonly keep Spanish stress, ex. (5) á.bwé.lí.tá 'granny' (stress on lí); the word for 'priest' [mɔ́h.kʰṍ] is said to have 'the wrong stress' (p. 9). Underlining (the stress mark) is lost in text extraction; verified visually.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: the lexical word / verbal stem; TAM-person proclitics excluded (ex. 19, ga=túk-i, bi=kád-i). Language is tonal (high, low, ascending) and the stress statement is made alongside the tone description; stress is treated as a phonological rule conditioning preaspiration. Citation-form vs. connected-speech not discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Palancar's 'Northern Otomi' is a dialect continuum covering Mezquital (Hidalgo, mezq1235), the Querétaro varieties (Santiago Mexquititlán, Tolimán, San Ildefonso Tultepec) and northern State of Mexico; the 2013 paper states (p. 2) that it is based on San Ildefonso Tultepec Otomi (Amealco, Querétaro), which is ISO otq = quer1236. Hekking's works describe Santiago Mexquititlán (also Amealco, otq). Two mis-assignments to flag: the Rosetta Project tags Hekking & Andrés de Jesús 1984 as 'ote' (Mezquital), and the local files the same grammar under mezq1235 — it is a Querétaro (Santiago Mexquititlán) grammar. The Wikipedia stress line (Blight & Pike 1976) concerns Tenango/Eastern Highland Otomi, not otq.

tone_statements.citation: Guerrero Galván, Alonso & Rafael Alarcón Montero. 2017. Estructuras tonales y variación dialectal del otomí: un estudio preliminar. In Leonor Orozco & Alonso Guerrero Galván (coords.), Estudios de variación geolingüística (Colección Lingüística, Serie Memorias), [chapter 12; includes pp. 344–352, full page range not seen]. Ciudad de México: Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia. 613 pp. ISBN 978-607-484-913-4.
tone_statements.quote: Generalmente esta lengua se describe como una lengua tonal, cuenta con dos tonos de nivel: alto (A) y bajo (B), y uno ascendente (BA) como se ejemplifica de (11-13) ... El tono sirve para marcar contrastes a nivel fonológico, tanto a nivel de la raíz como de la palabra. Según los datos revisados, solo en la sílaba tónica se dan los tres contrastes fonológicos ... la distribución del tono ascendente, limitado a las raíces, también se extiende al grupo clítico, el cual solamente recibe tonos de nivel ... considero que el otomí se acerca más a una lengua tono-acentual
tone_statements.translation: This language is generally described as a tonal language; it has two level tones, high (A) and low (B), and one rising (BA), as exemplified in (11-13) ... Tone serves to mark contrasts at the phonological level, both at the level of the root and of the word. According to the data reviewed, only in the stressed syllable do the three phonological contrasts occur ... the distribution of the rising tone, limited to roots, also extends to the clitic group, which only receives level tones ... I consider that Otomi comes closer to a tone-accentual language
tone_statements.locator: p. 249, tone section after Figura 1, with exx. (11)–(13) and Tabla 13 on p. 250; and p. 258, Conclusiones; also Introducción p. 236. (form-feed page = page).
tone_statements.summary: Three tones (high, low, rising), all contrasting only on the stressed root syllable; clitics bear only high vs low; demarcative root stress (length, intensity); F0 data; author: near tone-accentual.

tone_statements.citation: Guerrero Galván, Alonso. 2015. Patrones tonales y acento en otomí. In Esther Herrera Zendejas (ed.), Tono, acento y estructuras métricas en lenguas mexicanas (Estudios de Lingüística 24), 235–260. México, D.F.: El Colegio de México, Centro de Estudios Lingüísticos y Literarios. ISBN 978-607-462-688-9. (Papers from the Coloquio Tono, Acento y Estructuras Métricas en Lenguas Mexicanas, COLMEX, 21 Feb 2012.)
tone_statements.quote: Otomi languages (Oto-Pamean) have three tones, but only two are relevant for our purposes: high (represented with an acute accent) and low (not represented). ... from the variety of Northern Otomi spoken in San Ildefonso Tultepec in the state of Querétaro. Here the tonal contrast of high vs. low that serves to create minimal pairs for lexical words (e.g. ’bóts’e (H) ‘religious offering’ vs. ’bots’e (L) ... is exploited in inflectional clitics dá vs. dà or gí vs. gì. ... The third tone is a raising tone that is not found in inflectional formatives, but only found in lexical roots.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 2 'Tone as a phonological property of grammatical markers', author-version pp. 3-4 with footnote 4 on p. 4; floating-tone statement sec. 3 p. 4
tone_statements.summary: Three tones: high vs low (lexical minimal pairs, also on inflectional clitics) plus a rising tone found only in lexical roots; 3rd-person possessor = floating high tone landing on the preceding mora.

sources.note: §1.1 (preprint p. 4): most lexical words are disyllabic; default rule = stress on the first syllable (ex. 3, stress shown by underlining); deviating words with second-syllable stress are lexically specified (ex. 4: pá.da 'vulture', bã.tsi 'child', gó.né 'dumb'); Spanish loans keep Spanish stress (á.bwé.lí.tá); p. 7 ex. (19): TAM/person proclitics are unstressed, stress falls on the first syllable of the verbal stem (= lexical root); words are trochaic (strong–weak). Data explicitly from San Ildefonso Tultepec Otomi (p. 2).

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Otomi language' (en), section Tone and stress, citing Blight & Pike 1976 (Tenango Otomi, IJAL 42:51-57).
sources.note: "Stress in Otomi is not phonemic but rather falls predictably on every other syllable, with the first syllable of a root always being stressed." — attributed to Blight & Pike 1976 on Tenango (Eastern Highland) Otomi, a different variety from otq; secondary and not variety-specific.
